chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: Whoever bequeaths one-third of his wealth and is then killed by mistake, the one-third of his blood money is included in his bequest.

key_terms.ثُلُثُ: One-third — the maximum proportion of one's estate permitted as a bequest (wasiyya) in Islamic law
key_terms.خَطَأ: Khata' — mistake/error, specifically referring to unintentional (involuntary) homicide in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.دِيَة: Diyya — blood money, the financial compensation prescribed for unintentional homicide, paid by the killer's 'aqila (male relatives)
key_terms.وَصِيَّة: Wasiyya — bequest, the testamentary disposition of one's property before death, limited to one-third of the estate

ai.seo_question: What happens to blood money (diyya) if a person who made a bequest is killed by mistake in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) transmits a legal ruling from Imam Ali (AS) addressing the intersection of bequest law and homicide law. When a person has already allocated one-third of their wealth as a bequest (the maximum permitted in Islamic law), and subsequently dies as a victim of unintentional homicide, the blood money (diyya) paid by the killer's family is treated as part of the deceased's estate — and accordingly, one-third of that blood money also falls within the scope of the original bequest. This ruling establishes that the diyya received posthumously is treated as part of the decedent's wealth at the time of the bequest.
